listeningScripts.title: Hiring a School Instrument
listeningScripts.text:
Officer: Good afternoon, County Music Service, instrument hire.
Caller: Hello — my son has started learning at school and we've been told to hire an instrument.
Officer: Certainly. Can I take your name?
Caller: Yes, it's Harriet Quigley. Quigley is Q-U-I-G-L-E-Y.
Officer: And a contact number?
Caller: 07533 908 461.
Officer: Which instrument does he need?
Caller: A cello. He's nine.
Officer: Then he'll want a three-quarter size rather than a full size. A full-size cello for a nine-year-old is the commonest mistake parents make, and it makes the instrument genuinely harder to play.
Caller: Three-quarter, then. What does it cost?
Officer: Hire is fourteen pounds a month, and that includes a case and a bow. Rosin and spare strings you buy yourself; they're a few pounds.
Caller: Is there a deposit?
Officer: Forty pounds, refundable when the instrument comes back in reasonable condition. Normal wear is expected — we're not looking for perfection.
Caller: How long can we keep it?
Officer: The hire runs by school term, renewed automatically unless you tell us otherwise. Most families keep an instrument two or three years and then either buy or move up a size.
Caller: What if it gets damaged?
Officer: Small repairs are covered. Anything major — a crack in the body, a broken neck — and we'd ask for a contribution, but never the full replacement cost. Please don't try to fix anything yourself; glue on a cello is very hard to undo.
Caller: Understood. When can we collect it?
Officer: Thursdays and Fridays, between two and five, from the music centre on Foundry Road.
Caller: And do we need anything with us?
Officer: Proof of address, and the letter from the school confirming he's having lessons. That's what makes the hire subsidised rather than commercial.
Caller: Right. Anything else?
Officer: Don't leave it in a car overnight in winter. Cold and damp do more damage to string instruments than children do.

listeningScripts.title: Climbing Centre Induction
listeningScripts.text:
Instructor: Evening everyone, and welcome to Gritstone Climbing Centre. I'm Marcus, and this induction is required before you climb here, even if you've climbed for twenty years elsewhere.

Let me explain why, because people find it irritating. Every centre's systems differ — how the ropes are rigged, where the auto-belays are, which walls are for what — and most accidents here involve experienced climbers doing something that was correct at their previous centre.

Membership is fifty-two pounds a month, or nine pounds fifty for a single session. Under-eighteens must be accompanied by a registered adult, and by that I mean an adult who has done this induction, not an adult who is present.

Now the part that matters. Bouldering is on the low walls with mats and needs no rope. Everything above four metres needs a rope, and to use the roped walls you must either pass our belay test or use an auto-belay. The belay test takes fifteen minutes and can be done at the end of tonight. Do not be offended by it — we test people who have belayed for decades, and we fail about one in ten, almost always for the same thing, which is taking a hand off the brake rope.

The layout. Coming through reception, the bouldering room is straight ahead of you through the archway — that's the largest space and where most people start. The roped walls are on the left, along the western side, with the auto-belays at the far end of them. The training area with fingerboards and weights is upstairs above reception, and the café is on the right of reception as you come in, looking into the bouldering room through glass. Changing rooms are behind the café on the eastern side.

Two rules. Never climb directly above or below another climber on the roped walls. And no bags, water bottles or phones on the matting — a bottle under a falling climber's ankle is the single commonest cause of a broken bone in this building.

listeningScripts.title: Acting on Draft Feedback
listeningScripts.text:
Tutor: So — you've both had feedback on your first drafts. Let's talk about what to do with it.
Nadia: Mine says "needs more critical engagement". I don't know what that means.
Tutor: It means you have described what your sources say and not evaluated it. You have "Smith argues X, Jones argues Y" and no sentence beginning "however" or "the weakness of this is".
Nadia: So I add criticism?
Tutor: You add judgement, which is not the same. Say which account fits the evidence better and why — criticism for its own sake reads as badly as none.
Tom: Mine says "structure unclear". The comment is on page four.
Tutor: Then the problem is probably on page one. A reader who is lost on page four usually took the wrong turning much earlier — normally because the introduction promised a different shape from the one the essay has.
Tom: Should I rewrite the introduction?
Tutor: Write it last. Finish the argument, then write an introduction that describes the essay you actually produced rather than the one you intended.
Nadia: How much of the feedback do we have to act on?
Tutor: All of it, in the sense of considering it. Not all of it, in the sense of obeying. If you disagree with a comment, you may leave the text as it is — but write a line in your covering note saying why. A defended decision is fine; an ignored comment looks like carelessness.
Tom: What about the small corrections — commas, references?
Tutor: Do those last and in one pass. If you fix commas while the argument is still moving, you will fix commas in paragraphs you later delete.
Nadia: And if two markers said different things?
Tutor: That happens more than we admit. Where they conflict, decide, and say which you followed. What you cannot do is average them, which produces an essay that satisfies neither.

listeningScripts.title: Why Road Deaths Fell
listeningScripts.text:
Lecturer: Road deaths in most high-income countries have fallen by something like three-quarters since their peak, at a time when traffic volumes rose substantially, and I want to look at how, because the explanation contradicts the intuition almost everyone starts with.

The intuition is that roads became safer because drivers became better — through education, campaigns and enforcement. Those things happened, and their measured contribution is modest. The larger share came from designing a system that tolerates the mistakes people were always going to make.

Vehicle design did much of it. Crumple zones absorb energy that would otherwise reach the occupants, seatbelts and airbags manage deceleration, and structures are designed to deform in a controlled sequence. None of this prevents a crash. All of it changes what a crash does to a person, which is a different objective and turns out to be a more achievable one.

Road design followed the same principle later and less completely. Removing roadside objects that a leaving vehicle would strike, separating opposing traffic with barriers, replacing crossroads with roundabouts that convert head-on conflicts into glancing ones, and narrowing lanes in towns so that speed falls without a sign being read — each of these accepts that vehicles will leave the carriageway and reduces the consequence when they do.

Speed is where the physics is unforgiving and the politics most difficult. The energy in a collision rises with the square of the speed, so the difference between thirty and forty kilometres per hour is not a third more energy but very nearly double, and pedestrian survival falls away sharply across exactly that range. Every measure that lowers urban speed is contested, and the evidence for its effect is among the strongest in the field.

I'll finish with the framing, because it is the transferable part. The old model asked who was at fault and stopped there. The current model asks what could have been arranged differently so that the inevitable error did not become a death — the driver still made the mistake, and the system decided the outcome. That shift, from blame to design, is the single idea behind most of the reduction, and it is now being applied, slowly and with resistance, in medicine and industrial safety for the same reasons.
